content: For younger adolescents aged 10 to 14 years, the recommendation for voluntary medical male circumcision (VMMC) was considered conditional due to limited evidence regarding the use of circumcision devices in this age group. A detailed discussion of offering VMMC to this demographic is provided in Chapter 3, along with GRADE tables, study summaries, and evidence profiles. Each circumcision device has unique characteristics, and a comprehensive quality assessment for each device type—collar clamp, elastic collar compression device, and surgical assist vice clamp—is included in the annex. Most clinical studies on circumcision devices for potential use in VMMC programs classified adverse events (AEs) by severity. Moderate AEs were those manageable by mid-level clinicians within the VMMC program, while severe AEs required prompt surgical intervention by an experienced specialist or referral to higher-level care. Evidence supporting recommendations focused on two types of in situ devices (a collar clamp and an elastic collar compression device) and one surgical assist device. However, further research is needed to demonstrate the safety and advantages of these devices, particularly for adolescents, when scaled up in routine healthcare settings. The quality of data on the efficacy, safety, and acceptability of circumcision devices was considered low due to indirectness and potential bias, as neither patients nor observers were blinded. A systematic review identified studies on the safety, efficacy, and acceptability of the collar clamp device. Twelve studies using the conventional placement technique (involving 3,535 clients) were conducted in Africa, while three studies on the no-flip method (involving 654 clients) were also reviewed. Evidence from these studies, relevant to VMMC programs for HIV prevention in East and Southern Africa, was supported by data from China. Eligibility studies in Africa reported that 6% of men eligible for circumcision with the collar clamp device could not undergo the procedure due to the unavailability of the correct ring size. No additional exclusions were reported for the no-flip method. The no-flip technique, developed in China, simplifies device placement by avoiding foreskin eversion over the ring's exterior. Circumcision was successfully achieved in nearly all clients who underwent device placement, with a low failure rate of 3 per 1,000 placements. Most failures occurred during initial use at new sites or in adolescents. With the no-flip technique, only one placement failure was reported among 664 procedures in Africa, due to outer ring slippage after foreskin removal. In all cases, wounds were closed using sutures. Adverse events were categorized as moderate or severe, with 7% of clients experiencing AEs. Severe AEs were less common than moderate ones. Oedema and hematoma were less frequent with the collar clamp device compared to conventional surgery. Limited evidence was available on infections, with 6% of clients experiencing severe pain, bleeding, or wound dehiscence. Cosmetic outcomes were assessed during healing or at final follow-up visits, with 97% of clients reporting satisfaction with penile appearance after circumcision using the collar clamp device. Healing time following circumcision with the collar clamp device was approximately one week longer than after surgery, as healing occurs by secondary intention rather than primary intention (as in surgical circumcision). The mean healing time with the no-flip technique was slightly shorter, possibly due to the younger age of clients in those studies. A small number of wound disruptions occurred several weeks after device removal, representing deviations from the normal healing process. Pain levels during device placement and the post-procedure period were similar to those reported with conventional surgery. However, some men reported higher pain levels during erections while wearing the device. Evidence on pain with the no-flip method was of very low quality. Topical anesthesia was compared to injectable local anesthesia in adolescents, with longer wait times for topical anesthesia to take effect. Healing with the collar clamp device required longer sexual abstinence compared to surgical methods. The elastic collar compression device (e.g., PrePex™) was studied in 21 studies involving 12,855 clients. The device was generally removed seven days after placement. Some clients were ineligible for circumcision with this device due to conditions such as phimosis, narrow foreskin, adhesions, or other penile abnormalities. Severe AEs, including tetanus, were reported with the elastic collar compression device, leading the WHO to recommend ensuring tetanus vaccination before its use. Acceptability of device-based VMMC was high among clients, with most reporting satisfaction and willingness to recommend the procedure. However, barriers included pain, healing time, and time off from work or school. Health care workers found device-based methods easier to perform, requiring less time and resulting in fewer complications compared to surgical methods. However, some expressed concerns about pain and slow healing with certain devices. Cost analyses indicated that device-based circumcision procedures were roughly equivalent in cost to surgical methods, though device costs and associated medical supplies increased overall expenses. The shorter procedure time for device-based methods reduced clinician time, partially offsetting these costs.
